title: Crafts & Making
description: Crafts and making, from tearing paper to design thinking: cutting, folding and gluing; clay and play dough; recycled-material making; origami and paper engineering; weaving, block printing and India's living craft traditions; sculpture and 3D design; textiles and sustainable materials; and craft as livelihood, heritage and design.

lessons.title: Snip, Snip, Stick!
objectives: Use safety scissors safely to cut along a line

explanation: Paper is a wonderful material for making. We can tear it into pieces, cut it with safety scissors and stick it with glue.
Scissors safety: hold them with the points facing down, walk slowly, cut away from your fingers and only cut paper. Always ask a grown-up for help.
A little glue goes a long way. Dot the glue, press the paper down and hold it for a few seconds.

story.title: The Paper Garden
story.text: Ivaan tore green paper into little strips for grass. He carefully snipped out a yellow circle for the sun, holding his scissors the safe way. Dot, dot, dot went the glue, and press, press, press went his fingers. Soon a whole paper garden bloomed on his page. "I made it myself!" he said.

explanation: Play dough is soft and squishy. We can roll it into balls (round) and snakes (long), flatten it into pancakes and pinch it into points.
Putting shapes together makes things: a big ball and a small ball make a snowman; a long snake curls into a snail.
Potters make pots from clay, which goes hard when it dries or is baked in a hot oven called a kiln.

lessons.title: The Paper Boat
objectives: Make valley and mountain folds
Follow steps to fold a paper boat
explanation: Origami is the art of folding paper into shapes without cutting or gluing. The word comes from Japanese: "ori" (fold) and "kami" (paper).
A valley fold folds the paper towards you, making a V like a valley. A mountain fold folds it away from you, making a peak like a mountain.
Careful folding means lining up the edges and pressing the crease firmly. A paper boat that floats is a classic first project that children all over the world, including India, make in the rain.

vocabulary.meaning: the Japanese art of paper folding

examples: Folding a paper boat for monsoon puddles.
A folded paper cup that holds water briefly.

story.title: Monsoon Boats
story.text: When the first monsoon rains came, Grandpa taught Ivaan to fold paper boats, just as his own grandfather had taught him. Fold, crease, open, tuck. They raced their boats in the stream along the lane. Ivaan's boat sailed all the way to the corner. "Some things never change," Grandpa smiled.

lessons.title: Over, Under, Over, Under
objectives: Weave using warp and weft on a card loom
Name famous Indian woven textiles
explanation: Weaving makes cloth by crossing threads over and under each other. The threads stretched tight on the loom are the warp; the thread woven across is the weft.
On a simple card loom, you wind string around notches to make the warp, then weave wool over and under. The next row goes under and over, so the threads lock together.

India has famous woven textiles: Paithani silk saris from Paithan in Maharashtra with peacock borders, Banarasi silk from Varanasi, Kanjeevaram silk from Kanchipuram, and Pochampally ikat from Telangana.

vocabulary.meaning: to cross threads over and under

examples: A paper mat woven from strips.

story.title: Aaji's Paithani
story.text: Aaji unfolded her wedding Paithani, shimmering purple and gold. "Weavers in Paithan worked many months on this," she said, pointing to the peacocks in the border. Ivaan traced the threads. "Over and under, just like my paper mat!" "Exactly," said Aaji. "But a little more practice."

lessons.title: Block Printing
objectives: Make a stamp and print a repeating pattern
Match Indian crafts to their regions
explanation: Block printing uses a carved block dipped in colour and pressed onto cloth or paper. Repeating the print makes a pattern.
In Rajasthan, Sanganer and Bagru are famous for hand block printing with wooden blocks and natural dyes. Ajrakh printing is a tradition of Kutch in Gujarat and Sindh.

India has many other crafts: Bidri metalwork from Bidar, Channapatna wooden toys from Karnataka, Kondapalli toys from Andhra Pradesh, and Warli painting from Maharashtra. Many have Geographical Indication tags.

vocabulary.meaning: a print made with a carved block

examples: Bagru prints with natural indigo.

story.title: The Printer's Rhythm
story.text: In Bagru, Ivaan watched an artisan press a carved wooden block onto cloth: dip, press, thump, lift. Dip, press, thump, lift. A row of perfect flowers appeared. "How do you keep them straight?" Ivaan asked. The artisan tapped his head. "Thirty years of practice — and a good eye."

lessons.title: Adding and Taking Away
objectives: Distinguish additive and subtractive sculpture
Build a sculpture using an armature
explanation: Sculpture is three-dimensional art. In subtractive sculpture, the artist removes material — carving wood or stone. In additive sculpture, the artist builds up material — modelling clay or welding metal.
An armature is a frame, often of wire, that supports a sculpture from inside, like a skeleton.

India has great sculpture traditions: the rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock in the 8th century; Chola bronzes made by the lost-wax method (still practised at Swamimalai); and Dhokra metal casting by tribal artisans.

vocabulary.meaning: an inner frame supporting a sculpture

examples: Carving soap with a spoon (subtractive).
A foil armature covered in clay (additive).

story.title: The Temple From One Rock
story.text: At Ellora, workers began at the top of a hill and carved downwards, removing an enormous amount of rock — estimated at around 200,000 tonnes — to reveal the Kailasa temple, complete with pillars, elephants and towers. Nothing was added; everything was taken away. Ivaan stared up. "They must have planned every chip."

lessons.title: Pop-Ups and Nets
objectives: Make a pop-up card using a mechanism
Draw and fold a net to make a 3D box
explanation: Paper engineering uses folds and cuts to make paper move or stand up. A simple pop-up uses a "box fold": two parallel cuts on a fold, pushed inward, make a step that rises when the card opens.
A net is a flat shape that folds up into a 3D shape. A cube has a net of six squares. Adding tabs lets you glue the edges together.
Packaging designers use nets to make boxes, and pop-up book artists engineer complex scenes that spring up from the page.

lessons.title: From Cotton Boll to Cloth
objectives: Compare natural and synthetic fibres
Explain the process from fibre to fabric, including khadi
explanation: Natural fibres come from plants (cotton, jute, linen) and animals (wool, silk). Synthetic fibres, like polyester and nylon, are made from petrochemicals.
Making fabric involves cleaning fibres, spinning them into yarn, weaving or knitting the yarn into cloth, and dyeing or printing it. Natural dyes come from plants like indigo and madder.

Khadi is hand-spun, hand-woven cloth. Gandhi promoted the charkha (spinning wheel) and khadi in the freedom struggle as a symbol of self-reliance (swadeshi) and as an alternative to imported mill cloth.
examples: Indigo-dyed cotton.
The charkha at the centre of the Congress flag of the freedom movement.

story.title: The Spinning Wheel Revolution
story.text: In the 1920s, Gandhi asked Indians to spin yarn every day on a charkha and wear khadi. Across the country, people from every background sat at spinning wheels. The humble wheel became a symbol of independence and sat at the centre of the Congress flag; when India adopted its national flag in 1947, the charkha was replaced by the Ashoka Chakra.

lessons.title: The Design Thinking Process
objectives: Apply the design thinking process to a real problem
Evaluate materials for sustainability
explanation: Design thinking is a process for solving problems creatively, popularised by the design firm IDEO and Stanford's d.school. Its stages are: Empathise (understand users), Define (state the problem), Ideate (generate ideas), Prototype (build quick models) and Test (try them and learn).
The process is a cycle, not a straight line — designers often go back and improve.
Sustainable design considers a product's whole life cycle: materials, energy, use and disposal. Designers ask: can it be repaired, reused, recycled or composted?

vocabulary.meaning: to understand another's feelings and needs

examples: Designing a lunch bag that doesn't leak.

She interviewed Aaji (empathise), defined the problem, sketched ten ideas and made a prototype from an old sari with padded handles. Aaji tested it; the handles were too thin. Zuri improved them. Aaji now uses it every market day.

lessons.title: Crafts, Fair Trade and GI Tags
objectives: Analyse challenges facing artisan economies
Evaluate fair trade and Geographical Indications as protections
explanation: Crafts are a major source of livelihood in India, employing millions of artisans, many in rural areas and many of them women. Artisans face competition from machine-made goods, middlemen who take most of the profit, and limited access to markets.

Fair trade aims to give producers fair prices, safe conditions and long-term partnerships. Cooperatives and organisations such as SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association, founded by Ela Bhatt in 1972) help artisans organise.

A Geographical Indication (GI) tag protects products linked to a place, such as Darjeeling tea (India's first GI, 2004–05) and Kolhapuri chappals. GI tags can prevent imitation, but critics note benefits do not always reach individual artisans.

vocabulary.meaning: a way of earning a living
trade ensuring fair prices for producers

examples: Kolhapuri chappals with a GI tag.
Women's embroidery cooperatives in Kutch.

story.title: The Chappal Controversy
story.text: In 2025, a European fashion house displayed sandals that closely resembled Kolhapuri chappals, sparking debate in India about credit and fair benefit for the artisans of Kolhapur. The episode raised questions about how GI tags, design credit and fair partnerships can protect traditional crafts in a global market.

lessons.title: Makers and Machines
objectives: Explain digital fabrication technologies
Evaluate how technology and traditional craft can work together
explanation: 3D printers build objects layer by layer from digital designs, usually from plastic filament. Laser cutters cut precise shapes from wood, card or acrylic. CNC machines carve materials automatically.
The maker movement celebrates people making, repairing and sharing designs — in makerspaces, fab labs and online. Open-source designs let anyone build and improve them.

Technology and craft can combine: designers use digital tools to help artisans prototype new products, while hand skills give objects character machines cannot copy. Questions remain about job loss, plastic waste and preserving skills.

vocabulary.meaning: designs shared freely to use and improve

examples: A 3D-printed prosthetic hand from an open-source design.

story.title: A Hand for Ananya
story.text: Volunteers at a makerspace downloaded an open-source design for a prosthetic hand, adjusted its size for a girl named Ananya, and printed it overnight. It cost a small fraction of a commercial prosthetic. As Ananya picked up a cup for the first time, the volunteers realised that sharing designs could change lives.
